title: Brooklyn: Native Fields, Colonial Claims and Forced Removal
summary: Brooklyn’s Native fields and shorelines became colonial claims through separate agreements, expanding settlement and war. A 1652 Nayack agreement explicitly required residents and descendants to leave; Lenape life and cultural return continue.

history_title: How control of the land changed
history_content:
Native places became colonial property claims

Brooklyn's bays, cultivated flats and wooded hills were places of Native life before they became farms and town lots in the Dutch colony. The surviving records describe several transactions involving named Native owners and colonial officials. They do not describe a single sale of everything now called Brooklyn. Nor does a document's assertion of permanent ownership tell the whole story of what Native people understood, retained or experienced afterward. Early Colonial Settlements: Native land agreements in Brooklyn

The cultivated flats and the men who benefited

In June 1636, the Dutch records assigned the middle of three flats to Jacobus van Corlear and the western flat to Andries Hudde and Wolphert Gerritsen. A separate July instrument assigned the eastern flat to Director Wouter van Twiller himself. The texts name Native owners and chiefs and describe land extending from a creek and valley toward the woods. These were valued agricultural landscapes, not vacant ground. The officials who recorded the instruments were also connected to the people receiving the land, including the colony's director. Early Colonial Settlements: Native land agreements in Brooklyn

A company claim along the East River

The August 1, 1638 record names Kakapoteyno, Menqueuw and Suwirau in an agreement benefiting the Dutch West India Company. Its tract ran from George Rapalje's plantation at Rinnegachonch toward Mespaechtes, with the East River and inland woods as bounds. Fernow identifies those water places as Wallabout Bay and Maspeth Kill. The listed consideration included cloth, wampum, kettles, axes and hatchets. The record's sweeping transfer language made a corporate property claim over a Native landscape; the goods list alone cannot explain the transaction's consequences. Early Colonial Settlements: Native land agreements in Brooklyn

War and settlement changed what paper claims meant

Dutch settlement expanded amid Kieft's War of 1643–1645. Kieft ordered attacks on Native people; the violence spread through the region and disrupted communities and settlements. Later town-building converted colonial claims into house lots, farms and common lands. In Bushwick, settlement planning in 1660 followed the much earlier Company deed. Land loss thus involved physical settlement and violence as well as written agreements. Dutch Breukelen: Where Brooklyn Began

Nayack: a written demand to leave

In November 1652, Cornelis van Werckhoven's agreement with Seiseu and Mattano described land extending behind Gowanus, across the hills and toward Gravesend and the sea. The record acknowledged a previous Company purchase for which payment remained due. A separate December 1 agreement named Mattano, Mattaveno and Cossikan. In return for further goods, it required Native residents and their descendants to leave the occupied land called Naieck immediately and never return to live within the described district. This clause makes the intended consequence explicit: removal from a place where people were still living. It should not be hidden behind a neutral label such as “land purchase.” Early Colonial Settlements: Native land agreements in Brooklyn

Lenape history did not end with removal

Lenape Center authors Joe Baker, Hadrien Coumans and Chelsea Kimura challenge accounts that treat colonial deeds as sufficient explanations of homeland loss. Their discussion emphasizes Lenape relationships, laws and the consequences of displacement. In his introduction to *Lenapehoking*, Baker connects that history to continuing families and cultural work. Lenape Center's 2022 exhibition at Greenpoint Library brought Lenape art and knowledge into public view in Brooklyn. Diaspora and return belong in this story alongside the documents of dispossession. Lenapehoking: An Anthology

Explore the 1638 East River Company claim landscape for a closer view of the tract and its later settlement.

Where Brooklyn’s families went

The last tract of Native land in Brooklyn was sold in 1684. Families camped in small settlements at Gowanus, Nayack and Canarsie. Many moved east to Rockaway, Massapequa and Hempstead; others followed the Nayack sachem Mattano to Staten Island and New Jersey; still others went north to the Hudson and Delaware valleys. Most descendants of Brooklyn’s first people now live in Delaware, Mohican and Munsee communities in New Jersey, upstate New York, Ontario, Wisconsin, Kansas and Oklahoma.

Robert S. Grumet, New World Encounters: Jasper Danckaerts’ View of Indian Life in 17th-Century Brooklyn (Brooklyn: The Brooklyn Historical Society, 1986), exhibition catalog: Brooklyn place identities, archaeology, Danckaerts’ observations, “The Brooklyn Indian Diaspora” and Brooklyn’s Native community.

whereintheworld_content:
The shaded area is present-day Brooklyn, used to bring several distinct land agreements and their consequences into one readable regional story. It is not the footprint of a single deed, a reconstruction of a Native boundary, or evidence that every Native right ended at once. The 1636 flats, 1638 East River tract and 1652 Nayack agreements describe different places. Their creek, woodland and marked-tree boundaries cannot simply be replaced with today’s borough line. Modern shoreline data locate the reader; filled wetlands and changed shores also differ from the seventeenth-century landscape. The map does not identify private homes, burial places or archaeological sites.

NYS Civil Boundaries: Counties Shoreline

At the Bushwick–Ridgewood and Highland Park edge, this regional reading area overlaps the neighboring Newtown history. The connecting outlines have been reconciled within the historical map’s approximate alignment. Their overlap links relevant histories; it is not a recovered colonial boundary or evidence of an additional Native sale. Read the neighboring Newtown history
